summary: In Greek mythology, the Pseudea (Ancient Greek: Ψεύδεα, Pseúdea) are the personifications of lies and falsehoods. They are counted among the children of Eris (Strife), born without a father, and are little more than abstractions whose identity is exhausted by the meaning of their name. They are listed by Hesiod in the Theogony alongside their sibling the Logoi (Tales or Stories), and are seldom personified individually elsewhere in Greek myth.
etymology: The name derives from the Ancient Greek common noun ψεῦδος (pseûdos), "lie" or "falsehood"; the plural form Ψεύδεα (Pseúdea) expresses the several forms of deceitful speech they embody.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: The Pseudea are listed by Hesiod in the Theogony among the offspring of Eris, the goddess of strife and discord, who herself was a daughter of Nyx (Night). According to this account Eris bears her children alone, with no father named.

Their siblings, the other children of Eris, include Ponos (Toil), Lethe (Forgetfulness), Limos (Famine), the Algea (Pains), Hysminai (Combats), Machai (Battles), Phonoi (Murders), Androktasiai (Manslaughters), Neikea (Quarrels), Logoi (Tales or Stories), Amphilogiai (Disputes), Dysnomia (Lawlessness), Ate (Ruin or Delusion), and Horkos (Oath).

sections.heading: Character
paragraphs: As personified abstractions the Pseudea are regarded as little more than allegorizations of the meaning of their name, with virtually no narrative or distinct attributes of their own. They embody false speech and deception in the abstract.

They are not notably personified outside the catalogue of Eris's children, and no individual cult or distinct worship of the Pseudea is recorded. They are closely paired with the Logoi, the personified Tales or Stories, who receive the same minimal treatment in the sources.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: As members of the brood of Eris, the Pseudea belong to a group of personifications that embody the harmful and divisive aspects of human life, understood as the consequences that flow from strife and discord. Their place in the catalogue links falsehood to quarrels, disputes, and broken oaths among their siblings such as the Neikea, Amphilogiai, and Horkos.

Hesiod's Theogony (lines 226–232) is the primary ancient source for the Pseudea, and the personification largely begins and ends with this passage; later Greek literature does not develop them as independent figures.
